# Module: genre checklists

Load only for fiction, incident postmortems, tickets, technical articles and long-form journalism. Each rule names its genre; the generic rules in core still apply.

Tags: strength (`hard` always · `default` unless an exception or the sensitivity says otherwise · `soft` preference) · kind (`ai-tell`, `clarity`, `both`, `procedure`).

### INT-031 · postmortem content
`soft · clarity · scope: prose · genre: postmortem · voice can override`

In an incident postmortem, give absolute times with timezone including wrong turns, state the failure mechanism at code or config level (or ask the team), present contributing factors as a causal chain, state counterfactuals honestly with impact in numbers, write action items as concrete changes with an owner and date, and cite artifacts (file:line, commit SHA, verbatim error text, link); cut self-praise and moralising endings.

- Exceptions: never invent a time, number or mechanism the incident data does not contain (INT-001); blameless means naming systems and roles as actors, not omitting them
- Example: ✗ Lesson learned: communication is key. The system worked as designed. → ✓ Deploy 14:02 UTC, cache keys collided at 14:07, alert fired 14:19; action: add the key prefix test (A. Ruiz, 15 Nov).

### INT-032 · ticket and issue content
`soft · clarity · scope: prose · genre: tickets · voice can override`

In tickets and issues, title the outcome rather than the activity, start where the title stops, list only non-obvious steps with exact commands, give bugs an exact repro (versions, commands, input, expected versus actual output, frequency), write testable acceptance criteria with the command and expected output, state priority and estimate bare, and leave template fields empty or N/A rather than filled with prose.

- Exceptions: follow the repo's own ticket template and severity labels (criterion 6)
- Example: ✗ Improve login: clean up the auth flow. → ✓ Login returns 401 for emails with a plus sign (v2.3.1; repro: POST /login with a+b@x.io).

### INT-033 · technical article evidence
`soft · clarity · scope: prose · genre: technical-articles · voice can override`

In technical articles, use real code examples that were run or label them as sketches, attach conditions to numbers (machine, version, dataset, runs) or omit the number, give figures a baseline the reader can size, and put non-corrective follow-ups in a dated update block while corrections edit the body with a dated note.

- Exceptions: never fabricate the conditions: ask or omit (INT-001, INT-002)
- Example: ✗ It is 3x faster. → ✓ It ran 3x faster on a 10 GB dataset, v2.1, 5 runs on one laptop.

### INT-034 · reporter stance and quotation handling
`default · both · scope: prose · genre: journalism · voice cannot override`

In reporting, do not deliver a verdict the reporting did not establish (name the documented disagreement instead of both-sides balance), keep the spoken texture of quotations, attribute with a plain verb, and never rewrite the speaker's words except at the user's request.

- Exceptions: quoted material is protected (INT-004)
- Example: ✗ Experts agree the policy is a failure, she exclaimed. → ✓ Two of the five economists interviewed called the policy a failure, she said.

### INT-035 · fiction thematic over-determination
`soft · ai-tell · scope: prose · genre: fiction · voice can override`

In fiction, do not let narration or dialogue spell out the theme, delete in-text explanation of a symbol and keep the symbol, stop weather or setting mirroring mood scene after scene, and let at least one scene or image exist for texture only.

- Exceptions: do not remove a symbol or theme the author clearly built the work around
- Example: ✗ The storm raged, just like her grief; she understood that loss makes us human. → ✓ Rain on the car roof. She kept the engine off.

### LEX-046 · fiction stock imagery and default names
`soft · ai-tell · scope: prose · genre: fiction · voice can override`

In fiction, replace stock sensory and body-reaction cliches, filter words (she saw, he felt), atmosphere signature phrases, over-used default character names and smell-heavy sensory padding with the specific detail of this story.

- Triggers: `she felt a chill`, `a shiver ran down`, `the air was thick with`, `let out a breath she didn't know she was holding`
- Exceptions: memoir and personal essay: filter words that report a real inner state stay (INT-003); a cliche kept in dialogue because the character would say it
- Example: ✗ She felt a chill run down her spine as she saw the door open. → ✓ The door opened and the hairs on her arms stood up.

### PRC-042 · fiction revision order
`default · procedure · scope: prose · genre: fiction · voice can override`

For fiction, assess the rubric features in five separate group passes (marking features with no occasion n/a), fill an architecture sheet before drafting, and revise deepest layer first (architecture, then discourse, then style), telling the user how deep the surgery goes before cutting.

- Exceptions: corpus human and AI values are references, not targets
- Example: ✗ Polish sentences while the plot shape is unchanged. → ✓ Fix architecture first, then discourse, then style.

### STR-056 · fiction plot and cast shape
`soft · ai-tell · scope: prose · genre: fiction · voice can override`

In fiction, give the plot an unpredictable shape: test each turning point for inevitability (would it recur across twenty regenerations?), let chance, other people or institutions decide some outcomes, allow partial or open endings, sever a link in an unbroken cause chain, keep a sparse, uneven cast graph and use at most one structurally atypical choice.

- Exceptions: apply model-specific narrative corrections only when that model wrote the story; confinement or a single location that is the premise; diagnose and propose only; never insert plot material the author did not write (INT-007)
- Example: ✗ The hero decides, accepts and understands in the last paragraph, and every account is settled. → ✓ The hero decides; the other plot thread ends unresolved and a second character never learns what happened.

### STR-057 · fiction scene craft
`soft · ai-tell · scope: prose · genre: fiction · voice can override`

In fiction, open inside the situation with one working detail rather than an establishing shot, introduce characters through action or speech, ground setting in what a character does with the space, and show emotion mostly through behaviour with embodied rendering kept for one or two peaks.

- Exceptions: dialogue proportion: give dialogue slightly more floor than exposition, with indirect speech mixed in
- Example: ✗ The morning was grey. Maria, a tall woman of forty, stood in the kitchen, sad. → ✓ Maria set two cups down, then put one back.
